title: How the trade war with Canada is hitting US states—and could sway midterm elections
gist: The US-Canada trade war, after talks failed, has concentrated retaliation pain on politically important US states ahead of November midterms, while autos and oil remain unsparred escalation risks; Canada is fast-tracking a West Coast oil pipeline to diversify away from the US.

insights.claim: After US threats of 50 percent tariffs on about $20 billion of imports and failed talks, Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion of US exports and the US imposed an import ban on certain Canadian goods, with neither side currently negotiating.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Expect continued escalation risk with no active negotiating track.

insights.claim: Canadian retaliation hits products where US exporters depend on Canada, such as toilet paper (over 75 percent of the market), Michigan kraft paper (100 percent), Alabama ovens (95 percent) and Wisconsin blue cheese (88 percent).
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Small-cap exporters in these niches face outsized revenue hits.

insights.claim: North Dakota sends 81 percent of its exports to Canada, and Michigan and Ohio depend heavily on Canadian demand for autos, machinery and metals, so further retaliation would hit them hardest.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Identify state-level exposure for regional economic and credit risk.
insights.locator: Certain states are on the chopping block

insights.claim: Over 60 percent of Americans, including 64 percent of independents, oppose tariffs on Canada, and Republicans such as Susan Collins and Mike Rogers are breaking with the administration in Maine and Michigan.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Midterm pressure raises odds of a tariff de-escalation or carve-outs.
insights.locator: Certain states are on the chopping block

insights.claim: Because the costs are unevenly distributed, Washington and Ottawa both have incentives to test how much pressure the other can absorb.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.locator: A politically (and economically) costly trade war

themes.theme: Autos and oil as escalation risks

insights.claim: Autos are just under 20 percent of USMCA trade and have been spared, yet the average US tariff rate on Canadian autos and parts rose from 0.2 percent in February 2025 to 9.2 percent in August this year, and applying Section 232 tariffs to all autos regardless of USMCA status could cost importers an additional $44 billion.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Auto supply chains are the main tail risk if the trade war escalates.

insights.claim: Canada is fast-tracking a West Coast Oil Pipeline carrying over one million barrels per day from Alberta to the Pacific to reduce reliance on the US market and reach Asia, building on the Trans Mountain expansion.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Structurally diverts Canadian crude away from US buyers over time.

insights.claim: US sanctions and tariff pressure on Russian and Iranian oil push major buyers to diversify suppliers, and Canada has the opening market, infrastructure and an unhappy US buyer to benefit.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Supports Canadian crude diversification and non-US export growth.

insights.claim: The trade war's opportunity cost is forgone cooperation on modernizing the integrated North American economy, resilience to Chinese excess capacity and Middle East instability.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Longer-term damage to auto supply chains, oil flows and Canada's alignment with non-US partners.
insights.locator: A politically (and economically) costly trade war
